artifacts_produced.deploy_evidence: STEP 2, first half -- the honest exit. The failure branch printed ERROR, re-uploaded the log, then fell through to `shutdown -h +2 &` and exited 0, so SSM recorded Success on 69 consecutive failed runs and 95 days of breakage were invisible. One line was missing. THE FIX IS THE ESTATE'S, NOT INVENTED (build ladder rung 2): of the 6 BD download documents with a failure branch, 4 already exit non-zero, and this copies their exact shape. Exactly one line inserted, asserted in the edit script: 59 -> 60 runCommand lines, every other line byte-identical. Deployed as SSM DocumentVersion 2 (Hash 0be92f2611... -> 5130ead6f5...), default moved to 2, and the live content at $LATEST -- the version the trigger Lambda pins -- was RE-READ by this seat rather than taken from the update call's success.

STEP 2, second half -- the reorder, authorized by 2.0.0_SA_COO~O's ruling on row Z-S17. The honest exit as the estate writes it STRANDS the runner: `exit 1` returns before `shutdown -h +2`, and it fired on the first real run. The shutdown is now armed ABOVE the failure branch, so a failing run reports Failed AND still stops. 60 -> 66 runCommand lines; asserted in the edit script that exactly one `shutdown -h` and one `exit 1` survive and no pre-existing line was dropped. Deployed as DocumentVersion 3 (Hash 5130ead6f5... -> 490af5249f...), default moved to 3, live re-read at $LATEST: shutdown at index 58, exit at 63, LIVE == REPO line by line, 66 lines. NO INSTANCE INTERACTION, which is the constraint the ruling placed on it.

NEVER-2 ledger for the honest-exit deploy and the ONE ad-hoc vendor-facing run. 6 legs, all closed with proof, CLOSED, sentinel removed. Opened BEFORE the act with its blast radius and BOTH expected branches named. ITS ROLLBACK WAS CORRECTED AT AUTHORING TIME AND THAT MATTERS: the obvious rollback for an SSM document is a default-version flip, and it would have rolled back NOTHING here, because the trigger Lambda calls send_command with DocumentVersion='$LATEST', not the default. Read out of the producer's own code rather than predicted from the API's shape.

NEVER-2 ledger for the reorder. 4 of 5 legs closed with proof; the document is live and verified at v3. HELD-SOVEREIGN-GATED, gate class EXTERNAL, on the Monday 2026-09-28 22:10Z scheduled fire, which is the remaining verify leg's evidence source and needs NO new vendor authorization. HELD rather than OPEN is the accurate state: every apply/deploy leg is proven, so nothing is half-landed, and the tool refused a HELD while an apply leg was open -- correctly, and it caught a leg I had mis-specified as apply when it was really the persistence commit.

mutant.description: No mutant was planted, and none was needed: THE WORLD SUPPLIED A REAL ONE. The producer fails every day, so the before/after comparison is against genuine failures rather than a synthetic one. The discriminating question is not 'did the run fail' -- it always fails -- but 'does SSM now say so'.
mutant.expected: Before the change, a failing run exits 0 and SSM records Success. After it, the same failure exits 1 and SSM records Failed. If SSM had still read Success, the one-line fix did not take.
mutant.observed: FIRED. Before: the last recorded invocation of the old document reads Status Success beside a log saying 'download_rc=1 merge_rc=99'. After: command 9ba8d9c9 reads Status=Failed, ResponseCode=1, beside a log saying the same 'download_rc=1 merge_rc=99'. Identical failure, identical log text, opposite verdict, one line of difference. A SECOND CONTROL FIRED THAT I DID NOT WANT: the ledger predicted the stranded-instance side effect before the act, and it happened -- i-0e6f6dc014fdcf1cd was left running with no auto-stop alarm (describe-alarms = []). The prediction was in the entry, so the outcome was a confirmation rather than a surprise, and it drove the v3 reorder.

The structural read -- exit-line index vs shutdown-line index across all six documents -- says 5 of 6 strand. A snapshot answered a question about a standing property, and it answered it wrongly.
